blocks.text:
Design the real-time comment system behind a live stream, the kind of feature that sits underneath a YouTube Live broadcast or a Twitter Space, where thousands or even millions of people are watching the same event at once and typing comments that everyone else watching needs to see almost immediately. The problem sounds a lot like Slack or WhatsApp at first glance: people are sending text, other people are receiving it. But the shape of the traffic is completely different. A Slack channel has at most a few thousand members. A single viral livestream can have a million people connected to the exact same room at the exact same moment, all watching the same firehose of comments scroll by. That one fact, a single room with a million simultaneous readers, is what should drive almost every design decision in this problem.

The goal is not to build a system that remembers every comment perfectly forever, the way Slack does for a work conversation people search through months later. The goal is to get a comment from one person's keyboard onto a million screens in under a second, survive the biggest traffic spike the platform has ever seen, and degrade gracefully rather than fall over when that happens.

blocks.text: A viewer watching a live stream should see comments appear in near real time as other viewers post them. A viewer joining partway through the stream should see a short window of recent comments so the conversation does not feel like it started from nothing. A user should be able to post a comment, subject to a rate limit that keeps any one person from flooding the room. Comments that violate content policy should be removed from view soon after they are posted, even if they were briefly visible before a moderation system caught them. The system should report a live, approximate count of current viewers and reactions on the stream.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter more than anything else here, and they trade against each other in ways worth being explicit about.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter more than anything else here, and they trade against each other in ways worth being explicit about.

blocks.alt: Scalability, availability, low-latency fan-out, eventual consistency, and graceful degradation

blocks.text: Scalability means the system has to handle the gap between an ordinary stream with a hundred viewers and a viral one with a million, without a human manually provisioning anything in between. Availability means one gateway server crashing should drop the connections attached to it, not take down the stream for everyone else. Low latency matters more than perfect ordering, a comment showing up a second late is fine, a comment showing up in a different order on two different viewers' screens is also fine, but a comment taking ten seconds to appear is not. Consistency here is deliberately loose: this is not a banking ledger, it is a stream of chat messages, and eventual, approximately-ordered delivery is the right trade for speed. And under genuinely extreme load, the system should degrade gracefully, meaning it samples or throttles rather than crashing.

blocks.text: Comments are optimistically shown to viewers first and moderated asynchronously afterward, since blocking every comment on a synchronous moderation check would add latency to every single message for the sake of catching the rare bad one. Comment ordering only needs to be approximately correct, strict global ordering across every viewer is not required. Comment history is retained for a bounded window, days rather than years, since old livestream chat has much less lasting value than a Slack conversation people search through for work context. A viewer count is an approximation refreshed periodically, not an exact real-time tally, since exact counting across a million connections is its own hard problem that is not worth solving precisely here.

blocks.text: Say the platform has ten million daily active viewers across all live streams combined, but the interesting number is not the average stream, it is the busiest one. A single viral stream, a major sports final or a celebrity announcement, could plausibly hold a million concurrent viewers in one room. Comment writes across the whole platform might average a few hundred per second, spiking to around two thousand per second during a major event. The number that actually threatens the architecture is not the write rate, it is the fan-out amplification: one comment on that viral stream needs to be delivered to up to a million open connections, essentially instantly. A write rate of two thousand per second sounds modest until you realize each of those writes, on the hottest stream, needs to multiply out to a million deliveries.

blocks.alt: Ten million daily viewers, a single viral stream peaking at a million concurrent viewers, two thousand writes per second at peak, with fan-out amplifying a single comment on the biggest stream to up to a million deliveries

blocks.text: The architecture splits cleanly into a write side and a read side, connected through a fan-out layer in the middle. On the write side, a commenter posts through a stateless Comment API, which checks a rate limit, then pushes the comment onto an ordered, per-stream write queue. That queue feeds two independent consumers: a persistence worker that writes the comment durably to a comment store, and a moderation worker that scans it asynchronously. On the read side, viewers hold long-lived WebSocket connections to realtime gateway servers, which subscribe to a pub/sub fan-out layer keyed by stream id. When a new comment is published, the fan-out layer pushes it to every gateway shard that has at least one viewer watching that stream, and each shard forwards it down the open sockets it owns.

blocks.alt: Full system: clients connect via WebSocket through an edge load balancer to gateway shards, and post comments via an API load balancer to the Comment API, which rate-limits, queues, persists, moderates, and fans out through a pub/sub layer back to the gateways

blocks.text: The single hardest problem in this design is not writing a comment, it is delivering one comment to a million open sockets fast. A flat pub/sub channel that every gateway shard subscribes to directly works fine at modest scale, but at a million subscribers a single publish would need to fan out to hundreds of gateway processes simultaneously, and a naive broker can become the bottleneck. The fix is a hierarchical fan-out tree: a comment is published once at the origin, forwarded to a small number of regional fan-out nodes, and each regional node forwards it to the gateway shards in its region, which then push it down their own open sockets. This is the exact same shape as a CDN's origin-to-edge distribution, applied to a live message stream instead of a cached file.

blocks.alt: One comment publish fans out through regional nodes to gateway shards, each of which pushes to the thousands of viewers connected to it

blocks.text: Viewers are routed to gateway shards by a consistent hash of the stream id, so all the viewers of an ordinary stream land on the same shard set and share one subscription to that stream's channel. A viral stream breaks this rule deliberately: instead of every viewer of that one stream landing on a single shard set, viewers are further split across many shard sets by a secondary hash of the viewer id, so no single shard is ever asked to hold all one million connections for one stream at once.

blocks.text: The POST endpoint is idempotent by client-generated comment id, so a client that retries a timed-out request does not risk posting the same comment twice. The WebSocket subscription is where almost all of the read traffic lives, and it deliberately has no equivalent polling REST endpoint, since polling a million clients on an interval would recreate the exact fan-out problem the WebSocket layer exists to solve.

blocks.text: The schema is intentionally small: a stream, its comments, its active viewer sessions, and the users who write comments.

blocks.text: Comment rows are append-only and never updated in place except for the moderationStatus field, which flips from visible to removed when a takedown happens. ViewerSession exists mainly for operational visibility, to answer "which gateway shard is this viewer connected to" during debugging and rebalancing.

blocks.text: The comment store is a wide-column, write-optimized database like Cassandra or DynamoDB rather than a traditional relational database, partitioned by stream id and clustered by timestamp. This matches the access pattern exactly: almost every read is "give me the most recent comments for this one stream", never a join across streams. A relational database would work at small scale but would need careful sharding to handle a viral stream's write volume, work that a wide-column store's partitioning already does by design. Old streams naturally age out of the hot working set, and a time-to-live policy on comment rows keeps storage bounded without a separate cleanup job.

blocks.alt: A comment is rate-limited, queued, acknowledged to the sender, then persisted and published to the fan-out layer, which pushes it to every subscribed gateway shard
A new viewer connects, is routed to a gateway shard, receives recent history from the comment store, and subscribes to the live fan-out channel for everything from that point forward

blocks.text: The happy path for posting a comment during a normal stream is fast: the rate limiter has tokens available, the queue accepts it immediately, and within a few hundred milliseconds it has been persisted and pushed to every viewer. The interesting failure scenario is a viral spike: comment volume on one stream jumps by two orders of magnitude in seconds. The write queue absorbs the burst since it is just appending to a partition, the persistence worker may lag slightly behind but catches up because it processes asynchronously, and the fan-out layer is where the real pressure shows up, since it now has to push each comment to a shard set holding a million connections instead of a few thousand. This is exactly the scenario the sampling strategy in section 24 exists for.

blocks.text: The only thing worth caching aggressively is the "recent comments" list a newly joining viewer needs, since a viral stream can have thousands of people joining every second and hitting the comment store directly for each one would overwhelm it.

blocks.alt: A joining viewer checks a Redis-cached list of the last 50 comments for that stream first, falling back to the comment store only on a cache miss

blocks.text: This cache is a capped-length list per stream id, trimmed as new comments arrive, so it never grows unbounded and never needs a separate eviction policy beyond the trim itself.

blocks.text: A single Kafka topic partitioned by stream id sits between the Comment API and everything downstream, and three independent consumer groups read from it: persistence, fan-out publishing, and moderation. Keeping these as separate consumer groups means a slow moderation pass never delays persistence or delivery, and a fan-out spike never blocks moderation from eventually catching up and issuing a takedown.

Keeping these as separate consumer groups means a slow moderation pass never delays persistence or delivery, and a fan-out spike never blocks moderation from eventually catching up and issuing a takedown.

blocks.alt: One partitioned topic, read independently by a persistence worker group, a fan-out publisher group, and a moderation worker group

blocks.text: WebSocket connections need sticky, long-lived routing, which is a different problem than balancing stateless HTTP requests. Global DNS routes a viewer to their nearest region, a regional load balancer picks a healthy gateway instance, and from there the connection is sticky for its entire lifetime, since a WebSocket cannot simply be re-routed mid-connection the way a stateless request can.
blocks.content: WebSocket connections need sticky, long-lived routing, which is a different problem than balancing stateless HTTP requests. Global DNS routes a viewer to their nearest region, a regional load balancer picks a healthy gateway instance, and from there the connection is sticky for its entire lifetime, since a WebSocket cannot simply be re-routed mid-connection the way a stateless request can.

blocks.alt: Global DNS routes by latency to a region, a regional load balancer picks an instance, and the connection stays sticky to that instance for its lifetime

blocks.text: Scaling here is really about scaling connection capacity, not request throughput. Each gateway instance has a practical ceiling on how many open sockets it can hold, and the system watches that number directly rather than a proxy metric like CPU.
blocks.content: Scaling here is really about scaling connection capacity, not request throughput. Each gateway instance has a practical ceiling on how many open sockets it can hold, and the system watches that number directly rather than a proxy metric like CPU.

blocks.alt: When a gateway shard crosses 80 percent of its connection budget, a new shard is spun up and new connections are routed onto it

blocks.text: The API and worker tiers scale on the more familiar throughput and queue-lag metrics, since they are stateless and easy to add capacity to on demand.
blocks.content: The API and worker tiers scale on the more familiar throughput and queue-lag metrics, since they are stateless and easy to add capacity to on demand.

blocks.text: The comment store's natural partition key, stream id, already spreads write load across nodes for the common case of many concurrent streams. The single stream that breaks this assumption is the viral one, whose comment volume alone could overload a single partition's owning nodes.
blocks.content: The comment store's natural partition key, stream id, already spreads write load across nodes for the common case of many concurrent streams. The single stream that breaks this assumption is the viral one, whose comment volume alone could overload a single partition's owning nodes.

blocks.alt: An ordinary stream is handled by one shard set; a viral stream's viewers are additionally split by a secondary hash so no single shard set bears its full connection or write load alone

blocks.text: The same secondary-hash trick used for gateway sharding in section 7.2 applies here: an unusually hot stream id is given extra partitions rather than being forced through the same single partition every other stream uses.
blocks.content: The same secondary-hash trick used for gateway sharding in section 7.2 applies here: an unusually hot stream id is given extra partitions rather than being forced through the same single partition every other stream uses.

blocks.text: This system deliberately picks availability and low latency over strict consistency, because the data itself does not need strong guarantees.
blocks.content: This system deliberately picks availability and low latency over strict consistency, because the data itself does not need strong guarantees.

blocks.alt: Comments are eventually consistent, tolerating roughly a second of reordering; viewer and reaction counts are treated as approximate, refreshed periodically rather than computed exactly in real time

blocks.text: A viewer seeing two comments swap order by a few hundred milliseconds, or a viewer count that is a few seconds stale, causes no real harm. Choosing strong consistency here would mean coordinating writes across the fan-out tree in a way that directly fights the low-latency goal that matters far more for this feature.

blocks.text: The failure that matters most is a gateway shard going down mid-stream, since it is holding real, live connections when it happens.
blocks.content: The failure that matters most is a gateway shard going down mid-stream, since it is holding real, live connections when it happens.

blocks.alt: When a gateway shard crashes, its connected viewers reconnect through the load balancer to a healthy shard, which resubscribes to that stream's fan-out channel on their behalf

blocks.text: Because the fan-out layer and comment store are independent of any single gateway shard, a shard crashing loses nothing durable, it only forces a brief reconnect for the viewers it was holding, which is a far better failure mode than losing comments.

blocks.text: The main abuse vector is spam and flooding, which the rate limiter exists specifically to blunt.
blocks.content: The main abuse vector is spam and flooding, which the rate limiter exists specifically to blunt.

blocks.alt: Each user has a token bucket for comment posting; an empty bucket rejects the comment and asks the user to slow down rather than accepting it

blocks.text: Beyond rate limiting, every WebSocket connection and API call is authenticated, and the asynchronous moderation pass exists precisely because pre-publish moderation would add latency to every comment for the sake of catching the rare violation, a trade this design makes deliberately in favor of speed.

blocks.text: The metric worth watching above all others is fan-out delivery latency per stream, since that number degrading is the earliest sign that a stream is going viral faster than the system has scaled to match. Alongside it: open connections per gateway shard, write queue lag per partition, and moderation queue lag, since a moderation backlog growing unbounded means bad comments stay visible longer than intended.

Alongside it: open connections per gateway shard, write queue lag per partition, and moderation queue lag, since a moderation backlog growing unbounded means bad comments stay visible longer than intended.

blocks.alt: A single hot stream overwhelming one shard set, the fan-out broker itself becoming a bottleneck, and a moderation worker falling behind under a comment surge

blocks.text: Every one of these is mitigated by the same underlying idea used throughout this design: split the hot thing further rather than scaling it as one unit, whether that thing is a shard set, a broker channel, or a worker pool.
blocks.content: Every one of these is mitigated by the same underlying idea used throughout this design: split the hot thing further rather than scaling it as one unit, whether that thing is a shard set, a broker channel, or a worker pool.

blocks.text: The single most interesting trade-off in this whole design is what happens when comment volume on one stream becomes so extreme that delivering literally every comment to literally every viewer is no longer realistic.
blocks.content: The single most interesting trade-off in this whole design is what happens when comment volume on one stream becomes so extreme that delivering literally every comment to literally every viewer is no longer realistic.

blocks.alt: Under normal volume every viewer sees every comment; under an extreme viral spike, viewers see a representative sample instead of the full, unthrottled firehose

blocks.text: Sampling trades completeness for stability: a viewer during a massive spike sees a fast-scrolling, representative slice of the conversation rather than a perfectly complete one, which is exactly the trade real large-scale chat systems make, since a completely accurate but frozen or lagging feed is worse than a fast, slightly incomplete one.

blocks.text: This is the same instinct behind load shedding in any high-traffic system: under true overload, doing less work per request and serving everyone something is better than doing all the work for a shrinking few while everyone else times out.
blocks.content: This is the same instinct behind load shedding in any high-traffic system: under true overload, doing less work per request and serving everyone something is better than doing all the work for a shrinking few while everyone else times out.

blocks.text: Comment data has a short useful life compared to most durable application data, so a time-to-live policy that ages old comments out of the hot store after a matter of days, rather than keeping them indefinitely on expensive storage, is a straightforward cost win with no real product downside. Gateway capacity is the other major cost lever, and since connection counts vary enormously between an ordinary stream and a viral one, auto-scaling gateway shards down aggressively during quiet periods avoids paying for peak capacity around the clock.

A viewer's connection drops and reconnects rapidly in a poor network, which should not be treated as spam or trigger repeated full history refetches.
A comment is moderated and removed after already being pushed to a million viewers, requiring a takedown signal to propagate through the same fan-out path as a new comment.
Two streams that are related, such as a main broadcast and a simulcast, may need to share one comment room, which the stream id partitioning scheme needs to accommodate cleanly.

blocks.text: Gateway deployments use a rolling, connection-draining strategy rather than an instant restart, since killing a gateway instance outright would drop every connection it holds at once; draining lets existing connections finish or migrate gracefully while new connections land on already-updated instances. Canary releases for the fan-out layer are especially important, since a subtle bug there could silently drop comments for a large slice of viewers without any obvious error, exactly the kind of failure that is easy to miss without deliberate monitoring.
blocks.content: Gateway deployments use a rolling, connection-draining strategy rather than an instant restart, since killing a gateway instance outright would drop every connection it holds at once; draining lets existing connections finish or migrate gracefully while new connections land on already-updated instances. Canary releases for the fan-out layer are especially important, since a subtle bug there could silently drop comments for a large slice of viewers without any obvious error, exactly the kind of failure that is easy to miss without deliberate monitoring.

blocks.text: Threaded replies within the comment stream would make sense for less time-sensitive formats like recorded premieres, though they add complexity that a fast-scrolling live chat mostly does not need. Personalized filtering, such as letting a viewer follow only comments from accounts they follow, is a natural extension once the base fan-out problem is solved. Multi-region active-active fan-out, rather than a single origin region publishing outward, would reduce cross-region latency further for a truly global audience.

items: Architecture: a write path (rate limit, queue, persist, moderate) and a read path (gateway shards subscribed through a hierarchical fan-out layer), meeting only at the fan-out step.
Capacity: ten million daily viewers, a single viral stream peaking near a million concurrent connections, and a fan-out amplification factor that matters far more than the raw write rate.
Database: a wide-column store partitioned by stream id, clustered by time, with a bounded retention window.
End-to-end workflows: comment write and viewer join, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Scaling: connection-count-driven gateway scaling, with viral streams deliberately split across extra shards by a secondary hash.
Trade-offs: eventual consistency and approximate counts over strict guarantees, and sampling over completeness under extreme load.
Production considerations: connection-draining rolling deploys and careful canarying of the fan-out layer specifically.
